items.title: I can define biochemical pathway
items.what: A biochemical pathway is a sequence of chemical reactions, each catalysed by a different enzyme, where molecules are progressively converted from an initial reactant to a final product.
items.why: This definition underpins all of metabolism — photosynthesis, cellular respiration, and digestion are all organised as pathways rather than single reactions.
items.example: In a four-step pathway A → B → C → D, enzyme 1 converts A to B, enzyme 2 converts B to C, and enzyme 3 converts C to D. Each step is a distinct reaction with its own enzyme.

subtopic.name: Biochemical Pathways
subtopic.what: A biochemical pathway is a series of enzyme-catalysed reactions in which the product of one reaction becomes the substrate for the next. Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are both examples of biochemical pathways.
subtopic.why: Understanding pathways explains how complex biological processes are broken into manageable steps, each controlled by a specific enzyme. It also explains how cells regulate their own chemistry through feedback mechanisms.

items.title: I can distinguish between a reactant (substrate) and a product in a biochemical reaction
items.what: A substrate (reactant) is the molecule that enters a reaction and binds to the enzyme's active site. A product is the molecule that results from the reaction and is released from the enzyme.
items.why: Distinguishing substrates from products is essential for reading and interpreting pathway diagrams and for understanding what each enzyme does.
items.example: In the catalase reaction, hydrogen peroxide (H₂O₂) is the substrate. Oxygen (O₂) and water (H₂O) are the products.

subtopic.name: Biochemical Pathways
subtopic.what: A biochemical pathway is a series of enzyme-catalysed reactions in which the product of one reaction becomes the substrate for the next. Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are both examples of biochemical pathways.
subtopic.why: Understanding pathways explains how complex biological processes are broken into manageable steps, each controlled by a specific enzyme. It also explains how cells regulate their own chemistry through feedback mechanisms.

items.title: I can explain how a product of one reaction becomes the substrate in the next reaction
items.what: In a biochemical pathway, the product released by one enzyme-catalysed reaction is not a final endpoint — it immediately becomes the input molecule (substrate) for the following reaction.
items.why: This chaining of reactions allows cells to carry out complex multi-step transformations that would be impossible in a single reaction.
items.example: In the pathway A → B → C → D, molecule B is both the product of reaction 1 (catalysed by enzyme 1) and the substrate of reaction 2 (catalysed by enzyme 2). It plays both roles simultaneously.

subtopic.why: Understanding pathways explains how complex biological processes are broken into manageable steps, each controlled by a specific enzyme. It also explains how cells regulate their own chemistry through feedback mechanisms.

items.title: I can explain how biochemical pathways can regulate themselves through negative feedback
items.what: In many pathways, a downstream product inhibits an enzyme earlier in the pathway, slowing or stopping production when enough product has accumulated. This is called negative feedback.
items.why: Self-regulation prevents wasteful overproduction of molecules, saving the cell time, energy, and raw materials.
items.example: In the pathway A → B → C → D, if D accumulates, it may bind to and inhibit enzyme 1, slowing the conversion of A to B and reducing further production of D.

items.title: I can describe enzymes as biological catalysts that lower activation energy
items.what: Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions by lowering the activation energy — the minimum energy needed for a reaction to proceed. They are not consumed in the reaction.
items.why: Without enzymes, most biochemical reactions would occur too slowly to sustain life. Lowering activation energy means more molecules have enough energy to react at any given moment.
items.example: The decomposition of hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen occurs very slowly without assistance, but the enzyme catalase dramatically accelerates this reaction at body temperature.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Structure and Function
subtopic.what: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, lowering the activation energy of reactions. Their function depends critically on the shape and charge of their active site and, in some cases, their allosteric site.
subtopic.why: Because enzymes are proteins, their 3D structure directly determines what substrate they bind and how well they work. Anything that changes their shape — temperature, pH, inhibitors — changes their activity.

items.title: I can explain the role of the active site in enzyme specificity
items.what: The active site is a region on the enzyme with a unique shape and charge that is complementary to one specific substrate. Only that substrate can bind and react.
items.why: Specificity means each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or type of reaction, allowing the cell to control which reactions occur and when.
items.example: The enzyme catalase has an active site that is complementary to hydrogen peroxide. Other molecules cannot fit the active site and therefore cannot be broken down by catalase.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Structure and Function
subtopic.what: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, lowering the activation energy of reactions. Their function depends critically on the shape and charge of their active site and, in some cases, their allosteric site.
subtopic.why: Because enzymes are proteins, their 3D structure directly determines what substrate they bind and how well they work. Anything that changes their shape — temperature, pH, inhibitors — changes their activity.

items.title: I can describe the role of the allosteric site
items.what: The allosteric site is a second binding site on an enzyme, separate from the active site. Molecules that bind here are not substrates — they alter the shape of the active site instead.
items.why: The allosteric site is the mechanism by which non-competitive inhibitors and regulatory molecules control enzyme activity without directly blocking the active site.
items.example: When a non-competitive inhibitor binds to the allosteric site, the active site changes shape so that the substrate can no longer fit, reducing enzyme activity.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Structure and Function
subtopic.what: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, lowering the activation energy of reactions. Their function depends critically on the shape and charge of their active site and, in some cases, their allosteric site.
subtopic.why: Because enzymes are proteins, their 3D structure directly determines what substrate they bind and how well they work. Anything that changes their shape — temperature, pH, inhibitors — changes their activity.

items.title: I can distinguish between catabolic and anabolic enzyme reactions
items.what: Catabolic reactions break large molecules into smaller ones and release energy. Anabolic reactions build larger molecules from smaller ones and require energy input.
items.why: Recognising whether a reaction is catabolic or anabolic allows you to predict whether energy is released or consumed, which is fundamental to understanding metabolism.
items.example: Cellular respiration is catabolic — glucose is broken down and energy is released. Building a dipeptide from two amino acids is anabolic — energy must be supplied to form the peptide bond.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Structure and Function
subtopic.what: Enzymes are proteins that act as biological catalysts, lowering the activation energy of reactions. Their function depends critically on the shape and charge of their active site and, in some cases, their allosteric site.
subtopic.why: Because enzymes are proteins, their 3D structure directly determines what substrate they bind and how well they work. Anything that changes their shape — temperature, pH, inhibitors — changes their activity.

items.title: I can describe the lock-and-key model of enzyme function
items.what: In the lock-and-key model, the substrate has a shape that is a perfect, rigid fit for the active site of the enzyme before binding occurs — like a specific key fitting a specific lock.
items.why: This model explains why each enzyme is highly specific to its substrate and why molecules with different shapes cannot bind.
items.example: If enzyme X has a triangular active site, only a substrate with a complementary triangular shape will bind. A square-shaped molecule will not fit and cannot be catalysed by enzyme X.

subtopic.name: Enzyme-Substrate Models
subtopic.what: Two models describe how a substrate binds to an enzyme's active site: the lock-and-key model, where the fit is rigid and pre-formed, and the induced-fit model, where the active site adjusts its shape upon substrate binding.
subtopic.why: These models explain enzyme specificity at a molecular level and help predict how changes to enzyme structure will affect function.

items.title: I can describe the induced-fit model of enzyme function
items.what: In the induced-fit model, the active site is not a perfect fit for the substrate initially. When the substrate binds, the enzyme changes its shape slightly to mould around the substrate, improving the fit.
items.why: The induced-fit model is considered more accurate for many enzymes and better explains how some enzymes can accommodate substrates with slightly varying structures.
items.example: Hexokinase, which catalyses the first step of glycolysis, undergoes a conformational change when glucose binds — the enzyme wraps around the glucose molecule rather than having a pre-formed perfect fit.

subtopic.name: Enzyme-Substrate Models
subtopic.what: Two models describe how a substrate binds to an enzyme's active site: the lock-and-key model, where the fit is rigid and pre-formed, and the induced-fit model, where the active site adjusts its shape upon substrate binding.
subtopic.why: These models explain enzyme specificity at a molecular level and help predict how changes to enzyme structure will affect function.

items.title: I can compare the lock-and-key and induced-fit models
items.what: Both models agree that the active site and substrate have complementary shapes and charges, and that binding leads to a reaction. They differ in whether the active site shape is fixed (lock-and-key) or flexible (induced-fit).
items.why: Being able to compare the two models is a common exam requirement and demonstrates a deeper understanding of enzyme-substrate interactions beyond a single simplistic description.
items.example: Lock-and-key: the active site shape is set before the substrate arrives. Induced-fit: the active site begins complementary but finishes as a tighter fit after the substrate binds and the enzyme adjusts.

subtopic.name: Enzyme-Substrate Models
subtopic.what: Two models describe how a substrate binds to an enzyme's active site: the lock-and-key model, where the fit is rigid and pre-formed, and the induced-fit model, where the active site adjusts its shape upon substrate binding.
subtopic.why: These models explain enzyme specificity at a molecular level and help predict how changes to enzyme structure will affect function.

items.title: I can describe the role of coenzymes in enzyme function
items.what: Coenzymes assist enzymes either by altering the shape of the active site to activate the enzyme, or by acting as electron carriers that transport electrons to the active site and transfer them to the substrate.
items.why: Without coenzymes, certain enzymes cannot catalyse their reactions, making coenzymes essential components of metabolic pathways like photosynthesis and cellular respiration.
items.example: NAD acts as an electron carrier in cellular respiration — it picks up electrons (becoming NADH) and delivers them to the next stage of the pathway, enabling continued energy extraction from glucose.

subtopic.name: Coenzymes
subtopic.what: Coenzymes are organic molecules (containing carbon) that assist some enzymes in carrying out their catalytic function. Unlike substrates, coenzymes are not consumed in the reaction and can be reused.
subtopic.why: Many enzymes cannot function optimally without their coenzyme. Understanding coenzymes is essential for later work on photosynthesis and cellular respiration, where NAD, NADP, and FAD play central roles.

items.title: I can name three examples of coenzymes and state where they are used
items.what: Three key coenzymes are NAD (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide), NADP (nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide phosphate), and FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide).
items.why: These three coenzymes appear throughout the VCE Biology course in the context of photosynthesis and cellular respiration, so being able to name and locate them is a baseline requirement.
items.example: NADP is used in photosynthesis to carry electrons from the light reactions to the Calvin cycle. NAD and FAD are used in cellular respiration during the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain.

subtopic.name: Coenzymes
subtopic.what: Coenzymes are organic molecules (containing carbon) that assist some enzymes in carrying out their catalytic function. Unlike substrates, coenzymes are not consumed in the reaction and can be reused.
subtopic.why: Many enzymes cannot function optimally without their coenzyme. Understanding coenzymes is essential for later work on photosynthesis and cellular respiration, where NAD, NADP, and FAD play central roles.

items.title: I can explain the effect of temperature on enzyme activity in terms of kinetic energy
items.what: As temperature increases toward the optimum, molecules move faster (higher kinetic energy), leading to more frequent and successful enzyme-substrate collisions and a higher rate of reaction. Above the optimum, the enzyme denatures.
items.why: Temperature is one of the most significant variables controlling enzyme-catalysed reactions in living systems, including the light-dependent reactions of photosynthesis.
items.example: For a typical human enzyme with an optimum around 37°C, raising the temperature from 10°C to 37°C increases collision frequency and reaction rate. Raising it to 50°C begins to break hydrogen bonds in the enzyme's tertiary structure, reducing activity.

subtopic.name: Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity
subtopic.what: Enzyme activity is influenced by temperature, pH, substrate concentration, and enzyme concentration. Each factor affects how often enzyme-substrate interactions occur or whether the enzyme maintains its functional 3D structure.
subtopic.why: Living organisms must regulate these factors to maintain enzyme activity within functional ranges. In photosynthesis and cellular respiration, these factors directly control the rate at which energy is captured or released.

items.title: I can distinguish between a denatured enzyme and an inactive enzyme
items.what: An inactive enzyme has temporarily stopped functioning — for example, due to low temperature — but will resume activity when conditions return to normal. A denatured enzyme has permanently lost its 3D structure and cannot recover.
items.why: This distinction is important because denaturation is irreversible, while inactivation is not. Confusing the two leads to incorrect predictions about whether enzyme function can be restored.
items.example: An enzyme cooled to 0°C is inactive — warm it back to 37°C and it works again. An enzyme heated to 80°C is denatured — its hydrogen bonds have broken, the active site is destroyed, and cooling it back down does not restore function.

subtopic.name: Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity
subtopic.what: Enzyme activity is influenced by temperature, pH, substrate concentration, and enzyme concentration. Each factor affects how often enzyme-substrate interactions occur or whether the enzyme maintains its functional 3D structure.
subtopic.why: Living organisms must regulate these factors to maintain enzyme activity within functional ranges. In photosynthesis and cellular respiration, these factors directly control the rate at which energy is captured or released.

items.title: I can explain the effect of pH on enzyme activity
items.what: Each enzyme has an optimal pH. On either side of this optimum, the enzyme denatures as hydrogen bonds break and the active site changes shape. Changes in pH can also alter the charge of the active site, affecting substrate binding.
items.why: Different environments in the body have very different pH values, so enzymes must be matched to the pH of their working environment to function correctly.
items.example: Pepsin in the stomach has an optimal pH of around 1.5–2, suited to the highly acidic gastric juices. Salivary amylase has an optimal pH of around 6.5, suited to the near-neutral environment of the mouth. Placing pepsin in a pH 7 solution would denature it.

subtopic.what: Enzyme activity is influenced by temperature, pH, substrate concentration, and enzyme concentration. Each factor affects how often enzyme-substrate interactions occur or whether the enzyme maintains its functional 3D structure.
subtopic.why: Living organisms must regulate these factors to maintain enzyme activity within functional ranges. In photosynthesis and cellular respiration, these factors directly control the rate at which energy is captured or released.

items.title: I can explain the effect of substrate concentration on enzyme activity, including enzyme saturation
items.what: Increasing substrate concentration increases the rate of reaction up to a point. Once all enzyme active sites are occupied — a state called enzyme saturation — adding more substrate has no further effect.
items.why: Enzyme saturation sets an upper limit on reaction rate for a given enzyme concentration. Understanding this is essential for interpreting graphs of rate versus substrate concentration.
items.example: If 10 enzyme molecules are present and substrate concentration is low, only some active sites are occupied. As substrate concentration rises, all 10 active sites become occupied. Adding more substrate beyond this point does not increase reaction rate — the enzymes are saturated.

subtopic.name: Factors Affecting Enzyme Activity
subtopic.what: Enzyme activity is influenced by temperature, pH, substrate concentration, and enzyme concentration. Each factor affects how often enzyme-substrate interactions occur or whether the enzyme maintains its functional 3D structure.
subtopic.why: Living organisms must regulate these factors to maintain enzyme activity within functional ranges. In photosynthesis and cellular respiration, these factors directly control the rate at which energy is captured or released.

items.title: I can explain the effect of enzyme concentration on the rate of reaction
items.what: Increasing enzyme concentration increases the rate of reaction if substrate is in excess (unlimited). If substrate is limiting, rate increases initially but then plateaus as substrate becomes the bottleneck.
items.why: In biological systems, cells can regulate reaction rates by controlling how much enzyme is produced via gene expression, making enzyme concentration a key regulatory tool.
items.example: If substrate is unlimited: doubling enzyme concentration roughly doubles the rate (more active sites available). If substrate is limited: doubling enzyme concentration initially helps, but the rate soon plateaus because there is not enough substrate to keep all the extra enzymes occupied.

subtopic.what: Enzyme activity is influenced by temperature, pH, substrate concentration, and enzyme concentration. Each factor affects how often enzyme-substrate interactions occur or whether the enzyme maintains its functional 3D structure.
subtopic.why: Living organisms must regulate these factors to maintain enzyme activity within functional ranges. In photosynthesis and cellular respiration, these factors directly control the rate at which energy is captured or released.

items.title: I can define competitive inhibition
items.what: Competitive inhibition occurs when a molecule with a similar shape to the substrate binds to the active site of the enzyme, blocking the substrate from binding. The inhibitor and substrate compete for the same site.
items.why: Competitive inhibition is a controllable and reversible form of enzyme regulation — its effect can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration, which has practical implications for drug design.
items.example: Ibuprofen acts as a competitive inhibitor of the enzyme COX (cyclooxygenase). It has a shape similar to the natural substrate arachidonic acid and blocks the active site, reducing the production of prostaglandins that cause inflammation.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Inhibition
subtopic.what: Enzyme inhibitors are molecules that reduce or block enzyme activity. Competitive inhibitors bind to the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind to the allosteric site and change the shape of the active site.
subtopic.why: Inhibition is a key mechanism for regulating metabolism. It is also the basis for many drugs and pesticides — understanding inhibition types allows researchers to design molecules that target specific enzymes.

items.title: I can define non-competitive inhibition
items.what: Non-competitive inhibition occurs when an inhibitor binds to the allosteric site (not the active site). This causes the active site to change shape so the substrate can no longer bind, reducing enzyme activity.
items.why: Non-competitive inhibition cannot be overcome by adding more substrate, making it a more absolute form of inhibition and a distinct mechanism from competitive inhibition.
items.example: Some nerve agents (such as organophosphates used as pesticides) bind to the allosteric site of acetylcholinesterase. The active site deforms and the enzyme can no longer break down the neurotransmitter acetylcholine, causing a dangerous build-up.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Inhibition
subtopic.what: Enzyme inhibitors are molecules that reduce or block enzyme activity. Competitive inhibitors bind to the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind to the allosteric site and change the shape of the active site.
subtopic.why: Inhibition is a key mechanism for regulating metabolism. It is also the basis for many drugs and pesticides — understanding inhibition types allows researchers to design molecules that target specific enzymes.

items.title: I can explain the effect of competitive inhibition on the rate of enzyme activity
items.what: A competitive inhibitor reduces enzyme activity by occupying active sites. However, increasing substrate concentration can outcompete the inhibitor and restore the rate of reaction toward its uninhibited maximum.
items.why: The reversibility of competitive inhibition has direct consequences for how drugs work in the body — dose and concentration of both drug and substrate matter.
items.example: If a competitive inhibitor is present and substrate concentration is doubled, the substrate molecules are more likely to reach and bind the active site before the inhibitor does. The rate of reaction increases compared to when substrate concentration was lower.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Inhibition
subtopic.what: Enzyme inhibitors are molecules that reduce or block enzyme activity. Competitive inhibitors bind to the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind to the allosteric site and change the shape of the active site.
subtopic.why: Inhibition is a key mechanism for regulating metabolism. It is also the basis for many drugs and pesticides — understanding inhibition types allows researchers to design molecules that target specific enzymes.

items.title: I can explain the effect of non-competitive inhibition on the rate of enzyme activity
items.what: A non-competitive inhibitor reduces enzyme activity by deforming the active site via the allosteric site. Increasing substrate concentration does not restore activity because the active site shape is altered regardless of how much substrate is present.
items.why: This makes non-competitive inhibitors particularly powerful as regulatory molecules or drugs — their effect is not diluted by increasing substrate levels.
items.example: In an experiment comparing competitive and non-competitive inhibitors, doubling the substrate concentration restores rate toward normal for the competitive inhibitor. For the non-competitive inhibitor, the rate remains depressed at approximately the same level regardless of substrate added.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Inhibition
subtopic.what: Enzyme inhibitors are molecules that reduce or block enzyme activity. Competitive inhibitors bind to the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind to the allosteric site and change the shape of the active site.
subtopic.why: Inhibition is a key mechanism for regulating metabolism. It is also the basis for many drugs and pesticides — understanding inhibition types allows researchers to design molecules that target specific enzymes.

items.title: I can compare competitive and non-competitive inhibition
items.what: Both types reduce enzyme activity by preventing the substrate from binding to the active site. Competitive inhibitors bind directly to the active site; non-competitive inhibitors bind to the allosteric site. Only competitive inhibition can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration.
items.why: Being able to compare both types is a common extended-response requirement and is necessary for interpreting graphs where substrate concentration is varied.
items.example: On a rate-versus-substrate-concentration graph, a competitive inhibitor shifts the curve right (higher substrate needed to reach the same rate) but the maximum rate is eventually reached. A non-competitive inhibitor lowers the maximum rate achievable, regardless of substrate concentration.

subtopic.name: Enzyme Inhibition
subtopic.what: Enzyme inhibitors are molecules that reduce or block enzyme activity. Competitive inhibitors bind to the active site, while non-competitive inhibitors bind to the allosteric site and change the shape of the active site.
subtopic.why: Inhibition is a key mechanism for regulating metabolism. It is also the basis for many drugs and pesticides — understanding inhibition types allows researchers to design molecules that target specific enzymes.

items.title: I can describe how competitive and non-competitive inhibition can be used in rational drug design
items.what: Rational drug design uses knowledge of an enzyme's active site or allosteric site to engineer molecules that selectively inhibit that enzyme. Competitive inhibitors mimic the substrate shape; non-competitive inhibitors are designed to bind the allosteric site.
items.why: Many modern medicines — including antibiotics, antivirals, and cancer treatments — work by inhibiting specific enzymes. Understanding the mechanism allows researchers to design more effective and selective drugs.
items.example: Researchers studying a bacterium that causes stomach disease could design a competitive inhibitor shaped like the substrate of the bacterium's critical enzyme, blocking its active site. Alternatively, they could design a non-competitive inhibitor targeting the allosteric site, permanently deforming the active site and stopping the enzyme regardless of substrate levels in the stomach environment.
